newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil lower house approves petroleum bill.
newsitem.headline: Brazil lower house approves petroleum bill.

text.p: The lower house of Brazil's Congress on Wednesday approved a bill that opens up state-controlled oil and gas monopolies to the private sector and is expected to attract billions of dollars in investments.

The bill, which now has to be approved in the Senate, sets down rules for companies seeking to compete or enter joint-ventures with state-owned petroleum giant Petrobras which has operated as a monopoly for the last 40 years.
"This law will mean more investment and more production of petroleum and will bring about a qualitative leap for Brazil's economy as a whole," said deputy Eliseu Resende who drew up the legislation.

In 1995, Congress approved a constitutional amendment ending the state's oil and gas monopoly as part of Brazil's program to encourage much-needed private investment in several areas of the economy. Before the reform can be put into effect, however, a regulatory law is needed.
Officials say Brazil needs about $5 billion a year to keep its petroleum industry growing adequately. But Petrobras invests only about half that amount.

President Fernando Henrique Cardoso recently said Petrobras was studying more than 100 proposals from private companies interested in joint-ventures. The projects would double Brazil's oil output of about 860,000 barrels per day and reduce Brazil's reliance on imported petroleum, he said.

Brazil has oil and gas reserves equivalent to 14.1 billion barrels, small compared with Mexico or Venezuela, with much of them in deep-water areas of the Atlantic Ocean. Nevertheless, Petrobras is ranked among the top 20 international oil companies in terms of turnover, with annual sales topping $24 billion.
The bill approved by the lower house Wednesday would create a new regulator to oversee the petroleum sector and end fuel price subsidies within three years.
A series of amendments to the bill, including one which would eliminate an article that prohibits the government from privatizing Petrobras, was due to be voted next week.
Left-wing opposition parties said the new law represented a threat to national security by opening the door to foreign companies who might not have Brazil's best interests at heart.
"It's not Brazil that will be discovering more oil, it will be the concession-holding companies who will be able to what they like with it," said Workers Party deputy Miguel Rossetto.
